name: Protein intake for hair

lead: The idea is that because hair is keratin, adequate dietary protein supports hair. References note deficiencies can show up in hair.
No studies were found testing extra protein for hair in people with normal intake.

paras: Hair is made of keratin protein, so growth is thought to depend on adequate nutrition.
References do not report specific harms; hair-loss references note evidence for supplements is insufficient, and deficiencies like iron or B12 are cited as causes of hair loss.

lead: Protein intake for hair is the idea that eating enough protein supports hair growth and quality, because hair is made largely of keratin. It is discussed in lifestyle sections of hair and looksmaxxing communities.

General hair-care references state that a balanced diet matters and that deficiencies often show first in hair, naming protein, iron, zinc, biotin and other nutrients as linked to dryness, shedding or weak hair, though much of that text is uncited.[1] The same reference says shampoos or vitamins have not been shown to noticeably change growth rate.[1]

Dermatology references list malnutrition, vitamin B12 deficiency and iron deficiency among causes of non-scarring hair loss, and state that supplements are not typically recommended for hair loss and that there is no evidence for biotin.[2]

sections.h: Reported links between nutrition and hair
paras: Hair-care references say deficiencies of nutrients including protein can appear in the hair, and that growth is about 1.25 cm per month.[1] Hair-loss references mention malnutrition and iron or B12 deficiency as less common non-scarring causes.[2]
A hair-loss reference says supplements are not typically recommended, and that for most alternative remedies evidence is insufficient.[2]
